newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing to mourn Deng with six-day fun palace ban.
newsitem.headline: Beijing to mourn Deng with six-day fun palace ban.

text.p: China has ordered entertaiment centres and nightclubs in the capital Beijing to close during the period of mourning for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, but not all are heeding the call, dance hall staff said on Friday.
Deng died late on Wednesday and authorities have ordered six days of official mourning until his funeral next week.
The nightlife ban was a mark of respect for the political patriarch responsible for 18 years of reform that brought capitalist vigour to Beijing's once-staid entertainment industry, they said.
But the Chinese capital's cultural commissars failed to inform all of Beijing's fun spots of the ban and some late-night entertainment centres remained open, they said.

"The Beijing Cultural Bureau issued a notice to ask all entertainment places to stop business from yesterday," said a worker at the Top Ten dance hall, a favourite spot for China's new breed of urban pleasure-seekers.

"If flags are at half mast across the world, how can we go on amusing ourselves?" said a staff member at the rival HotTop Disco Club, which offers dance floors, live music and karaoke services for the affluent.
"We stopped business today in line with the order and will reopen after Deng Xiaoping's funeral on February 25," she said.

Under the strict rule of Deng's predecessor Mao Zedong, Beijing nightlife was almost a contradiction in terms. Restaurants were few and closed early. Western pop music was considered a capitalist disease.
Almost two decades of market-driven reform under Deng have transformed the entertainment scene.

All-night eateries and bars have proliferated and luxurious pleasure centres have mushroomed as entrepreneurs and state-owned firms rush to relieve the growing urban middle class of some of its new wealth.
Not all were planning to heed the government's call to shut up shop, with staff saying they had yet to be informed of the ban.
"We are still doing business, we don't know anything about this order," said a worker at a fashionable disco where trendy young Chinese mingle with foreign businessmen and students.
Officials of the Beijing Cultural Bureau were not available to comment on the ban, which workers said included the city's cinemas.
China has struggled to regulate the vigorous but sometimes shady entertainment sector.
